title: DeepMind's Chinchilla: why 70B parameters beat 280B on the same compute
summary: Chinchilla upended the old rule that more compute mostly means bigger models: model size and data should grow together, at roughly 20 tokens per parameter. We unpack the learning-rate bias in the old experiments, the three estimation methods and the three-way loss decomposition, hand-calculate an IsoFLOP valley, then list the numbers that don't add up in the paper and the new considerations after LLaMA.
ai_summary: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (DeepMind, 2022) trained more than 400 models and used three methods to estimate the optimal allocation under fixed compute. The conclusion is consistent: model size and training data both scale roughly with the 0.5 power of compute, at about 20 tokens per parameter, rather than Kaplan et al.'s 0.73 and 0.27. The difference comes mainly from the old experiments using the same learning-rate schedule for all models. Trained accordingly, 70B-parameter Chinchilla used Gopher's compute to see 1.4 trillion tokens, reached 67.6% on MMLU, and outperformed the 280B-parameter Gopher on nearly everything. The paper has several internal inconsistencies; later, LLaMA factored in inference cost and chose to train smaller models for longer.
brief: Problem: with a fixed compute budget, how big should the model be and how much data should it see? At the time, large models kept adding parameters while training data stayed around 300 billion tokens.
Method: train more than 400 models and estimate the optimal allocation three independent ways: the lower envelope of training curves, IsoFLOP valleys, and a three-term loss decomposition.
Result: model size and data should grow together, at roughly 20 tokens per parameter; 70B Chinchilla beats 280B Gopher on the same compute.
Caveats: large-scale validation rests on only one model pair, with confounds such as different optimizers; inference cost is ignored, and several numbers are internally inconsistent.

paper.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
paper.authors: Jordan Hoffmann, Sebastian Borgeaud, Arthur Mensch, Elena Buchatskaya, Trevor Cai, Eliza Rutherford and 16 other authors, 22 in total

big.label: Training tokens per parameter at the compute-optimal point

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually does

blocks.p: In March 2022, 22 DeepMind authors published this 36-page paper. It revisits the question from our earlier close reading of Scaling Laws: **with a fixed compute budget, how big should the model be, and how much data should it be trained on?**

Two years earlier, OpenAI concluded that more compute should mostly go into larger models, with data growing only slowly. This paper reruns the experiment with more than 400 models and reaches a very different answer: **model size and training data should grow in equal proportion**—double one, double the other. By their estimate, a compute-optimal run uses about 20 training tokens per parameter.

By that standard, the large models of the time were all underfed: GPT-3, Gopher, MT-NLG and other 100B-plus models were mostly trained on about 300 billion tokens. To test the idea, the authors used **exactly the same compute** as Gopher (280B parameters) to train a model with only 70B parameters but 1.4 trillion tokens, named Chinchilla. It beat Gopher on nearly every benchmark, raising MMLU from 60.0% to 67.6%. It is also four times smaller, making it much cheaper to run.

This paper changed how the industry trains large models. Labs stopped just adding parameters and started pushing training data into the trillions of tokens; later, they even trained models deliberately longer than "compute-optimal," because a smaller model is cheaper to deploy.

callout.title: In one sentence:
callout.text: With a fixed compute budget, the optimal model size N and number of training tokens D both scale roughly with the 0.5 power of compute: double the model, double the data, at about 20 tokens per parameter. Three independent estimation methods reach the same conclusion, and 70B-parameter Chinchilla beats 280B-parameter Gopher on the same compute.

callout.title: Four small concepts to know before reading
callout.text: You don't need deep background; these four will do:
list: **Loss and power laws**: loss measures how badly the model predicts the next token; it falls as a power law with model size and data. See our close reading of Scaling Laws for details.
**Training compute ≈ 6ND**: training an N-parameter model on D tokens takes about 6 × N × D floating-point operations. So for fixed compute, N and D trade off against each other.
**IsoFLOP**: "same compute." An IsoFLOP curve holds compute fixed and varies model size (with token count varying accordingly) to see which combination gives the lowest loss.
**Cosine learning-rate schedule**: the learning rate declines from a high value along a cosine curve. Its cycle length must be chosen in advance—one of the paper's key points.

sections.h: The problem: everyone added parameters, but not data

blocks.p: In 2020, Scaling Laws advised that every 10× increase in compute should scale the model about 5.5× but the data only about 1.8× (as quoted by this paper). Big models in the following two years largely followed that recipe: parameters grew from 175 billion to 530 billion, while training data stayed around 300 billion tokens:

fig.title: The largest models of the time: parameters kept growing, data barely moved
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 1; "tokens per parameter" is this site's calculation. Amber is Chinchilla

blocks.p: Why does this matter? The compute budget for training a large model is usually fixed in advance: how many accelerators you have and how long you can run them. Such models can usually be trained only once, so if you get the size or duration wrong, there is no second chance.

sections.h: Key finding: a hidden bias in the previous paper's experiments

blocks.p: The paper identifies a flaw in the experimental design of Scaling Laws: it gave every model **the same training length and learning-rate schedule** (a cosine decay to a fixed token count), then used mid-training losses to represent what a model would achieve if trained for only that many tokens.

The problem is that a cosine schedule only "finishes" when it completes its full cycle; the loss drops fastest at the end. If the schedule is designed for 130 billion tokens, stopping at 20 billion leaves the learning rate high and the model unfinished, so the loss is higher than for a model trained to completion on a schedule designed for 20 billion tokens. As a result, training on less data is systematically underestimated, pushing the conclusion toward more parameters and less data.

callout.title: Like timing a 10K run at marathon pace
callout.text: A runner starts at marathon pace, and you clock them at the 10-kilometer mark; that time will be slower than if they raced a 10K, because they're conserving energy and not sprinting. Concluding "this person is bad at short distances" would be unfair. The old experiments made exactly this mistake by using mid-training losses to represent shorter training runs.

blocks.p: The paper confirms this: if the cosine cycle is more than 25% longer than the actual training steps, the model is noticeably worse. So every experiment here matches the learning-rate cycle to the training length (with the learning rate decaying 10× over the run). Two other differences: the models are larger, mostly above 500 million parameters and up to 16 billion, whereas most of the older models were small, many under 100 million. The paper also finds that the compute–optimal-size relationship bends slightly at larger scales, so extrapolating from small models is biased.

quiz.q: Why does measuring mid-training loss with a learning-rate schedule designed for longer training underestimate the value of training on less data?
options: Because the learning-rate cycle hasn't finished; the model hasn't "settled," so mid-training loss is higher than for a model trained to that length on purpose
Because the model has fewer parameters mid-training
Because it hasn't seen the test set yet
quiz.why: A cosine schedule lowers the learning rate near the end, and that's when loss drops most. Stopping mid-cycle leaves the learning rate high and the loss elevated. If you treat that as "what a model can achieve with this much data," you overestimate the loss of training on less data and therefore underestimate its value. Parameter count doesn't change during training, and the test set has nothing to do with training progress.

sections.h: Method 1: draw the lower envelope of all training curves

blocks.p: The first method is the most direct. Take a set of models (70 million to over 10 billion parameters), train each size four times, with learning-rate cycles matched to four different training lengths whose longest and shortest differ by 16×. Plot all training curves on a compute–loss chart; at each compute value, find the curve with the lowest loss, and record its model size and tokens seen.

callout.title: What the lower envelope is
callout.text: Overlay dozens of training curves falling from upper left to lower right, then trace along their bottom edge. That line is "the lowest loss achievable at each compute budget." Each point on it corresponds to a specific model size and data volume—the optimal combination for that compute.

blocks.p: After sampling 1,500 logarithmically spaced compute values, they fit power laws for optimal model size and optimal token count as a function of compute: N_{opt} ∝ C^{a}, D_{opt} ∝ C^{b}. The result is **a = 0.50, b = 0.50**: the two grow exactly in step. The paper also notes that every selected point falls in the final 15% of its training run—another sign that the learning-rate cycle should match training length.

sections.h: Method 2: fix the compute, find the loss "valley"

blocks.p: The second method is more intuitive. Choose nine compute budgets (from 6 × 10^{18} to 3 × 10^{21} FLOPs), and under each train a range of model sizes: the larger the model, the fewer tokens it gets, so the budget is used exactly. Then look at final loss as a function of model size.

Under each budget, loss shows a clear valley: models too small can't absorb the data; models too large don't get enough data. The valley floor is that budget's optimal model. The paper fits a parabola to each curve to locate the bottom, then connects the bottoms with power laws, obtaining **a = 0.49, b = 0.51**.

fig.title: With Gopher's compute, how to split it: the middle is best, both ends are worse
fig.subtitle: Schematic: this site's calculation from the Method 3 fitted formula and rounded parameters, with compute = 5.76 × 10^{23} and D = C / 6N. Not empirical data. Amber marks the area near the valley floor.
fig.note: The valley floor is fairly flat: the difference between 20B and 70B is small, but 280B is clearly worse. With rounded parameters, the minimum is around 32B; the paper's unrounded parameters give about 40B. The "predicted loss" also includes an irreducible constant of 1.69, discussed in Method 3.

quiz.q: On an IsoFLOP curve, why does an overly large model end up with higher loss?
options: Because larger models overfit the test set more easily
Because with fixed compute, a larger model gets fewer training tokens and is undertrained
Because large models have too small a learning rate
Because large models use a different architecture
quiz.why: Compute ≈ 6ND is fixed, so when N goes up, D must fall in proportion. A larger model has more capacity, but with too little data the "undertrained" loss grows quickly and outweighs the benefit of capacity. In these experiments each example is seen only once, so there is no issue of memorizing the test set.

sections.h: Method 3: split loss into three terms and solve directly

blocks.p: The third method pools all the experiments from the first two methods and fits a formula with an explicit interpretation:

parts.desc: The data's own "entropy": the loss that cannot be removed even with a perfect model and infinite data. Language itself has irreducible uncertainty
Loss from the model being too small: even a perfectly trained Transformer with N parameters falls this far short of the ideal model
Loss from insufficient training: seeing only D tokens, each once, leaves this much gap to a fully trained model
The two exponents determine how quickly returns come from adding parameters and adding data

formula.note: The fit uses a Huber loss that is insensitive to outliers (δ = 10^{-3}) and the L-BFGS optimizer, choosing the best result from a set of initial values to avoid local minima. The paper says a larger δ makes the fit cater too much to small-compute experiments and worsens predictions for large ones.

blocks.p: These three terms come from a classic decomposition: total loss = ideal floor + gap from "limited model capacity" + gap from "imperfect training." With this formula, you can hand-calculate the predicted losses of two models:

fig.title: Hand-calculated from the formula: with the same compute, Chinchilla's predicted loss is lower
fig.subtitle: Schematic: this site's calculation from the fitted formula in Appendix D.2; not measured data. The blue column is total predicted loss.
fig.note: Gopher's "model capacity" term is already small (0.052), so adding parameters barely helps; its "not trained enough" term is 0.251. Chinchilla shifts some budget from parameters to data: the first term rises by only 0.03, while the second falls by nearly 0.09.

blocks.p: **The condition for optimal allocation.** Minimizing loss under fixed compute 6ND gives an elegant result: at the optimum, the ratio of the two reducible loss terms equals β : α, or A/N^{α} : B/D^{β} = 0.28 : 0.34. In plain terms: **the next unit of compute must buy the same loss reduction whether it goes to parameters or to data**; otherwise you should shift budget toward the higher-return side. The optimal exponents follow directly:

formula.expr: N_{opt} ∝ C^{a}, D_{opt} ∝ C^{b},  a = β / (α + β),  b = α / (α + β)

parts.desc: The exponent for how fast the optimal model size grows with compute
The exponent for how fast the optimal data volume grows with compute. a + b = 1, because N × D is proportional to compute
The two exponents are similar, so a and b are both close to 0.5: model and data grow in lockstep.

formula.note: The paper reports Method 3 gives a = 0.46, b = 0.54, and predicts an optimal model of about 40 billion parameters at Gopher's compute. Using the paper's rounded parameters, a = 0.28 / 0.62 ≈ 0.45 (see "Where the paper doesn't add up" below).

blocks.p: As an aside, E = 1.69 is very close to the roughly 1.7 nats that the earlier paper guessed for the entropy of language. But the two papers use different datasets and tokenization, so the values aren't directly comparable—just an interesting coincidence.

quiz.q: In L(N, D) = E + A/N^{α} + B/D^{β}, which term cannot be eliminated no matter how much model capacity and data you add?
quiz.why: E represents the irreducible uncertainty of text itself (the same context can be followed by many plausible words); it remains even with infinite model and data. A/N^{α} tends to 0 as the model grows, and B/D^{β} tends to 0 as data increases.

quiz.q: At optimal allocation, why must the marginal loss reduction from adding parameters equal that from adding data?
options: Because the formula requires α = β
If one side had higher returns, shifting a bit of compute from the lower-return side would lower total loss—so the original allocation wasn't optimal
Because parameters and data cost the same per unit
quiz.why: This is a general principle for any budget-allocation problem: if two ways of spending have different marginal returns, there is room to improve until they are equal. α and β are not equal (0.34 vs. 0.28), so at the optimum the two loss terms are in the ratio β : α, not 1 : 1.

sections.h: Three methods, one conclusion: model and data grow together

fig.title: All three methods find a ≈ b ≈ 0.5, far from the old conclusion
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 2; parentheses are 10th and 90th percentiles estimated by bootstrap. The blue column is the data exponent b
rows: Method 1: lower envelope of training curves
fig.note: The paper also re-runs Method 2 on the C4 and GitHub code datasets, getting 0.50 / 0.50 and 0.53 / 0.47 respectively; the conclusion is the same.

blocks.p: The three methods use different fitting procedures and different models, yet their conclusions are nearly identical. Method 3 predicts a somewhat smaller optimal model; the paper explains that its Huber loss automatically treats low-compute experiments as outliers and gives more weight to high-compute points, and that the compute–optimal-size relationship bends slightly downward at large scales.

**About 20 tokens per parameter.** Table 3 lists, using Method 1, how much data each model size needs to be compute-optimal: 1B parameters needs about 20.2B tokens, 10B needs about 205.1B tokens, and 67B needs about 1.5 trillion. Work out the ratios and they all land around 20 (this rule of thumb is calculated by this site from the table; the paper's main text does not state it this way).

fig.title: How much data and compute a model needs to be compute-optimal
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 3 (Method 1). "Tokens per parameter" is this site's calculation; "Gopher units" means how many times the compute used to train Gopher. Amber is the optimal point at Gopher's compute.

blocks.p: The implication is stark: a 175B-parameter model needs several trillion tokens to be trained well, while GPT-3 used only 300B. A compute-optimal 1-trillion-parameter model is not worthwhile unless you have more than 250× Gopher's compute. The paper therefore stresses that **larger, higher-quality datasets** will be the key to further scaling language models.

quiz.q: Using the rule of thumb of about 20 tokens per parameter, about how many tokens should a 7B-parameter model be trained on to be compute-optimal?
quiz.why: 7B × 20 = 140 billion tokens. 1.4 trillion is Chinchilla's data volume (70B parameters); 300 billion was the "standard" training volume for large models at the time. Later, many 7B-class models were actually trained on far more than 140B tokens; see the end of the article.

sections.h: Validation: training Chinchilla on Gopher's compute

blocks.p: All three methods put the optimal model for Gopher's compute between 40B and 70B parameters. For dataset and computational-efficiency reasons, the authors chose the upper end: **70B parameters, 1.4 trillion tokens**, using the same compute as Gopher.

fig.title: Chinchilla and Gopher: same layers, half the width
fig.subtitle: From paper Table 4; batch size doubles midway through training. Amber is Chinchilla.

blocks.p: Beyond size and data volume, the two differ in several ways, all listed in the paper:

list: **Data mixture**: both use the MassiveText dataset, but because Chinchilla trains on more tokens, the sampling proportions of the subsets were slightly adjusted, and parts of the web and Wikipedia subsets are seen more than once.
**Optimizer**: Chinchilla uses AdamW, Gopher uses Adam. The paper finds that AdamW improves language-modeling loss and downstream task performance.
**Tokenizer**: it removes a text-normalization step (NFKC); the vocabulary is 94.15% identical to Gopher's, which helps represent mathematical and chemical symbols.
**Numerical precision**: forward and backward passes use bfloat16, but a float32 copy of the weights is kept in the optimizer state.

callout.title: This is not a "change one variable" controlled experiment
callout.text: Differences in optimizer, tokenizer, and numerical precision could all make Chinchilla stronger. The appendix separately compares Adam and AdamW and confirms that AdamW is better on its own. So strictly speaking, part of Chinchilla's margin over Gopher cannot be credited to better compute allocation. The paper also runs a cleaner controlled comparison at small scale: at 10^{21} FLOPs, the old method recommends 4.68B parameters and the new method recommends 2.86B; trained with identical settings, the model predicted by the new method is better.

sections.h: Results: nearly across-the-board wins over Gopher

blocks.p: The paper compares Chinchilla with Gopher—and with GPT-3, MT-NLG 530B and others—on language modeling, reading comprehension, question answering, common sense, MMLU, BIG-bench and many other tasks. Most attention went to MMLU, an exam-style benchmark covering 57 subjects:

fig.title: MMLU 5-shot average accuracy: 70B-parameter Chinchilla clears 60% for the first time
fig.subtitle: Units: %; from paper Table 6. Amber is Chinchilla; "2023 forecast" is the average prediction made in 2021 by a group of professional forecasters for the best score by June 2023.

blocks.p: Chinchilla is 7.6 points above Gopher, and even beats the forecasters' average expectation for June 2023. Across the 57 subjects, it is better on 51, tied on 2, and worse on only 4 (college mathematics, econometrics, moral scenarios, formal logic).

fig.title: Other representative tasks: mostly clear wins
fig.subtitle: From paper Tables 7–9 and the main text; units: accuracy %. The blue column is Chinchilla.
fig.note: On the common-sense task PIQA, both score 81.8%. On RACE, GPT-3 and MT-NLG used different prompt formats, so the paper explicitly notes they cannot be directly compared.

blocks.p: Two details worth noting. First, Chinchilla also leads on language-modeling tests such as The Pile, but the paper cautions that it saw 4× more data, raising the risk that test-set content leaked into training data; it therefore gives more weight to tasks like MMLU and BIG-bench that are less leakage-prone. Second, zero-shot TruthfulQA improves by 14.1 points. Earlier research had suggested that larger models were less truthful; the paper argues this shows that **simply learning the pretraining data better** can clearly improve truthfulness.

**Bias and toxicity.** On Winogender, which measures whether pronoun resolution is influenced by gender stereotypes, Chinchilla is more accurate than Gopher on every group, but male pronouns improve by only 3.2 points, while female and neutral pronouns improve by 8.3 and 9.2 points—an uneven gain. On toxicity, the average score of 25,000 unprompted generations is 0.087, versus 0.081 for Gopher, a negligible difference: a better language model is not necessarily more toxic, nor necessarily less toxic.

sections.h: Where the paper doesn't add up

blocks.p: The paper's conclusions are solid, but many details are internally inconsistent. We list them one by one; worth keeping in mind when reading the original:

list: **MMLU score**: the abstract says 67.5% and "over 7 percentage points"; the main text and Table 6 say 67.6% and 7.6 percentage points higher.

**How much compute and data a 175B-parameter model needs**: the main text says 4.41 × 10^{24} operations and more than 4.2 trillion tokens, while Table 3—which it cites—says 3.85 × 10^{24} and 3.7 trillion. For the 280B-parameter model, the main text says about 10^{25} operations and 6.8 trillion tokens, while Table 3 says 9.90 × 10^{24} and 5.9 trillion. The main text also disagrees with the Method 2 and Method 3 tables in the appendix.

**Appendix Table A3 appears to be off by one order of magnitude**: in the Method 3 column, the compute for the 175B-parameter model is written as 1.26 × 10^{24}, smaller than the 1.71 × 10^{24} for the 67B model in the row above. Checking with 6ND: 175B parameters × 12 trillion tokens × 6 ≈ 1.26 × 10^{25}, so this is likely a typo.

**Method 3 exponents**: Table 2 gives a = 0.46, but the 10th–90th percentile interval in parentheses is (0.454, 0.455); the point estimate is outside its own interval. From the paper's α = 0.34 and β = 0.28, a = 0.28 / 0.62 ≈ 0.45, which matches the interval.
**Training data range**: the abstract says models were trained on 5B to 500B tokens; the introduction says 5B to over 400B.
**GPT-3 size**: the discussion section writes GPT-3 as 170B parameters; everywhere else the paper says 175B.
**Gopher's compute**: the main text uses the older figure 5.76 × 10^{23}, while the appendix uses a more precise method and gets 6.3 × 10^{23}.

callout.title: Later, researchers went back and checked the paper
callout.text: In 2024, researchers at Epoch AI tried to reproduce Method 3 and argued that the reported parameters were inconsistent with the first two methods and that the confidence intervals were implausibly narrow. This is the same kind of problem as the mismatch between the a value and the interval above. But the core conclusions of Methods 1 and 2—that model and data grow in roughly equal proportion—remain widely accepted.

blocks.p: Limitations listed in the paper itself:

list: **Only one large-scale validation pair**: because of cost, only Chinchilla and Gopher could be compared at large scale; there is no further validation at intermediate sizes.
**Power-law assumption**: the observed optimal model size bends slightly downward at large compute, meaning the paper may **still overestimate** the optimal model size at high compute.
**Single pass over the data**: all experiments train for less than one epoch with no repeated data; multiple-epoch training was not studied.

**Data quality**: the paper speculates that scaling datasets only helps if quality is high; trillion-token web data contains more toxicity, bias and private information, and test-set leakage is harder to audit.

blocks.p: **What happened next.** Chinchilla's conclusion was quickly adopted by the industry, but then a new consideration appeared: **inference cost**. In February 2023, Meta released LLaMA. The paper opens by noting that Chinchilla's objective considered only the training budget and ignored the inference budget; if a model is to be deployed at scale, a smaller model trained longer is ultimately cheaper. By Chinchilla's advice, a 10B-parameter model should be fine with 200B tokens, but LLaMA found that a 7B-parameter model kept improving after 1 trillion tokens. Since then, training small models far beyond the compute-optimal point has become the norm in open-source models.

So Chinchilla answers "what is optimal when the training budget is fixed," while the real world also has to count the cost of running the model many times. Understanding that distinction is key to understanding today's crop of small but strong models.

sections.h: Test yourself: did you get it?

quiz.q: Kaplan concludes N ∝ C^{0.73}; Chinchilla says N ∝ C^{0.5}. If compute increases 100×, how much should the optimal model scale under each conclusion?
quiz.why: 100^{0.73} ≈ 29 and 100^{0.5} = 10. Under Chinchilla, the remaining 10× goes to data; under Kaplan, data grows only 100^{0.27} ≈ 3.5×. Exponents are not multipliers—you raise the base to the exponent.

quiz.q: Why do Chinchilla's authors believe MMLU and BIG-bench are more informative than language-modeling scores on The Pile?
options: Because The Pile is too easy
Because Chinchilla saw 4× more data, raising the risk that test content leaked into training data, so language-modeling scores may be inflated
Because Gopher was not evaluated on The Pile
quiz.why: With more data, the training set is more likely to contain the same texts as the test set, inflating language-modeling scores through memorization. Exam-style tasks are relatively less affected by this kind of leakage, so the paper places more weight on them. This is a caveat the paper itself raises in the main text.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What is the difference between Chinchilla's and Kaplan's conclusions? What is the main source of the difference?
Why does measuring mid-training loss with a learning-rate schedule designed for longer training underestimate training on less data?
How do the three methods estimate the optimal allocation? Why is the IsoFLOP curve a valley?
What do the three terms in L(N, D) = E + A/N^{α} + B/D^{β} represent?
At optimal allocation, why is the ratio of the two reducible loss terms β : α?
Where does "about 20 tokens per parameter" come from? Under what assumptions does it hold?
Which factors in Chinchilla's win over Gopher cannot be credited to compute allocation?
Why did LLaMA later deliberately train longer than compute-optimal?
